## Installation

`seny` is a Bioconductor package; install it with `r Biocpkg("BiocManager")`:

```{r install, eval = FALSE}
if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE)) {
    install.packages("BiocManager")
}
BiocManager::install("seny")
```

## What seny does

For every cluster-by-contrast comparison in a multi-sample single-cell dataset,
`seny` decides whether a pseudobulk differential-expression test is **Adequate**,
**Underpowered**, **Caution** or **Invalid**, and explains why. The diagnostics
are analytic and run on your own data; there is no per-dataset simulation. The
variance model and power follow the DE method you intend to run:
`r Biocpkg("edgeR")` (default), `r Biocpkg("DESeq2")` or `r Biocpkg("limma")`
voom.

The call has a severity order --- Invalid > Caution > Underpowered > Adequate ---
and a `reason` string that lists *every* flag, so a single headline never hides a
second problem:

| Call | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Invalid** | Type I error cannot be trusted (design not estimable, too few samples per group). |
| **Caution** | Valid, but a specific risk applies (condition confounded with a covariate, cell-count imbalance tracking the condition under DESeq2, or a subtype shift inside the cluster that would make genes look DE on its own). |
| **Underpowered** | Valid but unable to detect the target effect (sensitivity too low, or too few testable genes). |
| **Adequate** | No flags. |

## The example dataset

`seny` ships a small simulated dataset: 24 donors (12 per condition), three cell
types, each planted in a different regime so the call varies. A finer annotation,
`cell_type_fine`, splits CD4 T into naive and memory subtypes; we come back to it
under *Composition*.

```{r load}
library(seny)
sce <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "example_sce.rds", package = "seny"))
table(sce$cell_type, sce$condition)
```

## Running the assessment

`assessAll()` chains the layers --- pseudobulk setup, design/confounding
(layer 1), pseudobulk quality (layer 2), variance structure and sensitivity
(layer 4) --- and returns one row per comparison.

```{r assess}
res <- assessAll(sce, sample = "donor", group = "condition",
                 annotations = "cell_type", targetLFC = 1)
```

The comparison table carries the layer-2 cell-quality metrics alongside the
call. `cells_cond_cor` is the correlation of log cells-per-sample with the
condition; `cells_ratio` is the smaller group median over the larger;
`expected_recall` is the share of true effects of the target size the test is
expected to detect (mean per-gene power at the target), and drives the
Adequate / Underpowered call.

```{r table}
cols <- c("cluster", "nA", "nB", "median_cells", "gini_cells", "cells_ratio",
          "cells_cond_cor", "n_testable", "expected_recall", "call")
knitr::kable(as.data.frame(res)[, cols], digits = 2, row.names = FALSE)
```

Each non-adequate call explains itself:

```{r reasons}
d <- as.data.frame(res)
for (i in seq_len(nrow(d))) {
    cat(d$cluster[i], "->", as.character(d$call[i]), "::", d$reason[i], "\n")
}
```

Here CD4 T is clean (**Adequate**). CD8 T has far fewer cells in condition B, so
its cell-count imbalance tracks the condition; seny reports it in the reason, but
the call stays **Adequate** because edgeR and voom remain calibrated under
imbalance. DESeq2 loses FDR control there, so with `method = "deseq2"` the same
comparison is **Caution**:

```{r deseq2}
res_d <- assessAll(sce, sample = "donor", group = "condition",
                   annotations = "cell_type", targetLFC = 1, method = "deseq2")
as.character(res_d$call[res_d$cluster == "CD8T"])
```

NK has high between-donor variance at a modest cell count, so few genes are
detectable at the target effect (**Underpowered**).

## The traffic-light matrix

`plotAdequacy()` renders the table as a clusters-by-contrasts grid, one plot per
annotation set, coloured by the call --- the at-a-glance view.

```{r matrix, fig.alt = "Traffic-light matrix of adequacy calls by cell type"}
plots <- plotAdequacy(res)
plots[["cell_type"]]
```

## Reading the diagnostics

A family of plotting functions explains the calls. `plotVariance()` shows where
each comparison's noise comes from --- the depth, cell and donor shares of the
per-sample variance. A donor-dominated bar means only more donors will help.

This attribution needs the cell-level overdispersion `theta`, fitted from the
single cells. It is off by default because it is the slowest step and the
calls do not use it; ask for it with `thetaReps = 3`:

```{r variance, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 3, fig.alt = "Variance attribution bars"}
res_theta <- assessAll(sce, sample = "donor", group = "condition",
                       annotations = "cell_type", targetLFC = 1, thetaReps = 3)
plotVariance(res_theta)
```

`plotRegime()` places the same decomposition on one triangle, coloured by the
call and sized by the median detectable effect: position shows where the noise
is, size shows how hard detection is.

```{r regime, fig.width = 5.5, fig.height = 5, fig.alt = "Variance regime ternary"}
plotRegime(res_theta)
```

`plotComparison()` assembles a single comparison --- the call and its reason, the
variance donut, the sensitivity curve and the cells per sample --- into one card.

```{r card, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 4, fig.alt = "Comparison card for one comparison"}
plotComparison(res_theta, "cell_type:NK:B_vs_A")
```

Other views: `plotConfounding()` (Layer-1 association), `plotCells()` (cells per
sample by condition), `plotSensitivity()` (detectable effect vs expression) and
`plotPower()` (power vs effect size).

## Composition: subtype shifts inside a cluster

A broad cluster often holds subtypes, and their shares can differ between the
conditions. Pseudobulk DE on the broad cluster then reports the subtypes' marker
genes as DE although no gene changes within any subtype. CD4 T looked
**Adequate** above, but its naive and memory subtypes shift with the condition:

```{r fine}
table(sce$cell_type_fine, sce$condition)
```

Give `assessAll()` both annotation levels. `seny` works out which level nests in
which from the cells, and for each broad cluster:

- tests the subtypes' shares of the cluster with propeller from
  `r Biocpkg("speckle")`;
- predicts, per gene, the log2 fold change the observed shift alone would cause,
  and the power to call it DE, which sums to the number of DEGs expected from
  composition alone;
- labels each DEG of the broad cluster's own test as *composition-driven*,
  *within-child DE*, *mixed* or *unresolved*, by comparing the observed change
  with the prediction and checking whether any subtype shows the gene as DE.

```{r composition}
res2 <- assessAll(sce, sample = "donor", group = "condition",
                  annotations = c("cell_type", "cell_type_fine"), targetLFC = 1)
d2 <- as.data.frame(res2)
cols <- c("annotation", "cluster", "call", "composition", "comp_child",
          "exp_comp_deg", "n_parent_deg", "n_comp_driven")
knitr::kable(d2[d2$annotation == "cell_type", cols], digits = 2, row.names = FALSE)
d2$reason[d2$comparison == "cell_type:CD4T:B_vs_A"]
```

CD4 T is now **Caution**: the memory share rises from about 40% to 66%, enough to
make about 44 genes look DE at the broad level. `plotComposition()` shows the shift and
which of the cluster's DEGs it explains: composition-driven genes sit on the
diagonal, while the genes that really change inside the subtypes do not.

```{r compplot, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 4.5, fig.alt = "Subtype shares and composition attribution for CD4 T"}
plotComposition(res2, "cell_type:CD4T:B_vs_A")
```

What to do with a composition Caution: test the subtypes separately (their own
calls are in the same table), or interpret the broad cluster's DEGs with the
attribution in hand. A cluster whose overall share differs between conditions is
reported (`share_A`, `share_B`, `share_fdr`) but not flagged, since that alone
does not bias DE within it. With a single annotation level the composition is
`"not assessed"`.

## Sharing the results

`reportSeny()` writes the whole assessment to one self-contained HTML file: a
summary of the calls and their reasons, the traffic-light matrices, a sortable
table of every comparison, the composition flags and a card per comparison
(flagged ones first, up to `maxCards`). It needs pandoc, which ships with
RStudio.

```{r report, eval = FALSE}
reportSeny(res2, file = "seny_report.html")
```

For an editable version, `rmarkdown::draft("my_report.Rmd", template =
"seny_report", package = "seny")` copies the template.

## Thresholds and honest reporting

The numeric cut-offs that drive the call live in `defaultThresholds()` and can be
overridden. They are **provisional placeholders** --- the final values are being
derived from a validation study (OneK1K, AIDA and an in-house atlas), not chosen
up front.

```{r thresholds}
str(defaultThresholds())
```

This run assessed `r nrow(d)` comparisons. When you scan many comparisons at
once, treat the matrix as a screen, not a ranking: picking the standout cell
after the fact inflates false positives. The call tells you which comparisons are
*worth* testing --- it does not replace multiple-testing control across them.

```{r session}
sessionInfo()
```
